transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-06-04 16:00 UTC | Duration: 42m
Attendees: Alicia Park (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Priya Shah (Quantile Head ML), Marcus Lee (Quantile SRE), Sana Iqbal (Quantile CTO)

Summary: quick round of bench numbers, routing triage, action items captured at end

[00:00] Alicia: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call, then we'll jump into the Week 3 bench readout. Diego, you want to kick off with the numbers?
[00:12] Diego: Yeah, thanks. So we ran the EU lab tests against your representative prompt set and the incumbent endpoint. Median latency for our quantized variant was 38 ms per token, incumbent was ~52 ms, so about a 27% median improvement under steady state. Throughput, sustained, we hit 320 rps on the 4-GPU pool vs 210 rps for the incumbent under the same concurrency profile.
[00:36] Priya: Sorry, can you repeat the throughput numbers, I missed the second one?
[00:40] Diego: Sure, 320 requests per second sustained for the workload shape you provided; incumbent averaged 210 rps.
[00:45] Marcus: Is that for your hosted routing or the dedicated slot runs? Which config?
[00:49] Alicia: These were hosted runs with routing pinned to the EU region using our quantized 8-bit optimized kernels. We also toggled prefix caching for common prompt prefixes.
[00:58] Marcus: Right, we noticed in our lab that during bursts the p95 jumped up, is that the same for you?
[01:04] Diego: Good call. Yes, p95 was higher under bursty tail events. Median is lower but the p95 was around 420 ms in one of the stress windows — we traced that to KV cache misses and lane contention when many concurrent sessions warmed KV cache simultaneously.
[01:20] Priya: K V cash? Do you mean KV cache?
[01:23] Diego: Sorry yes KV cache, the transcription on my notes says K V cash but it's KV cache.
[01:26] Sana: Are those KV cache misses a config we can tune on our side or something Redwood needs to control?
[01:31] Diego: It's a mix. We can adjust the cache warm policy and prefetch heuristics on the runtime; you can also change how many concurrent sessions you open in the warm window. For the head-to-head we recommend a short pre-warm step to reduce tail spikes.
[01:43] Alicia: To be practical, we proposed two routing plays: 1) keep requests in-hosted EU with prefix caching and a 1-minute pre-warm for heavy windows, or 2) use a dedicated slot with pinned capacity for your 22:00-02:00 batch window. Dedicated removes most noisy-neighbor variance but costs are predictable.
[02:01] Marcus: What's the observed delta in tail behaviour if we go Dedicated?
[02:05] Diego: In our sims, moving to Dedicated reduced p95 by about 30% in burst tests — p95 fell from ~420 ms to ~290 ms, medians changed minimally.
[02:14] Priya: That seems reasonable. Budget question though — Sana, how much runway do we have for dedicated?
[02:19] Sana: We have a small envelope for pilot scale but we'll need an explicit cost/benefit summary before committing. Can Redwood provide per-hour cost / estimated unit cost numbers for Dedicated vs Hosted?
[02:28] Alicia: Absolutely. We'll send a cost ladder and unit economics breakdown for both modes; Diego will include the effect of batching and quantization on token unit price.
[02:35] Marcus: Also, the EU region we tested was eu-west-2. Can we replicate in eu-central-1? Our prod is in Frankfurt.
[02:41] Diego: We can run the same bench in eu-central-1 — kernel selection differs slightly on that hardware but results should be comparable; we'll mark that as part of the head-to-head.
[02:49] Priya: On the incumbent side they use a custom sharding + mem-caching approach. Any notes on how Redwood's KV cache differs?
[02:57] Diego: Our runtime uses a distributed KV cache with short-lived prefix entries and optional sticky routing so repeated conversations hit the same cache shard. Incumbent's mem-cache looked more aggressive on session pinning which helps baseline at low concurrency but hurts multi-tenant churn scenarios.
[03:12] Priya: Okay. Can you show the charts?
[03:14] Alicia: Yep, I'll share screen — Diego, you can narrate.
[03:18] [03:18] Screen share: Median latency bar chart, throughput time-series, p95 waterfall
[03:25] Diego: So here you can see the median improvement, the throughput sustained curve, and then the p95 spikes during the 30s burst windows. The annotated spikes line up with KV cache cold starts.
[03:38] Marcus: There's a brief spike at 10:42 in the trace you showed — is that an artifact of the test harness?
[03:44] Diego: That spike correlates with our simulated auth token refresh in the harness — we accidentally used a shorter token TTL in that run. Not representative. We re-ran without the short TTL and the p95 improved ~8% in that window.
[03:59] Priya: So after removing the harness artifact, we still see residual tail variance. What's the practical mitigation strategy?
[04:05] Diego: Two prongs: routing/playbooks + runtime knob. Routing: smooth bursts with short pre-warm and small admission control; runtime: increase KV cache size and reduce eviction aggressiveness for heavy windows. We also suggested a small client-side connection pool to avoid connection churning.
[04:23] Alicia: Operationally for the head-to-head we recommend three runs: baseline workload, a 5-minute burst overlay at 3x normal QPS, and an overnight 3-hour sustain test. We'll run both in eu-central-1 and eu-west-2.
[04:36] Marcus: Time window? We prefer 22:00-02:00 UTC for minimal prod interference.
[04:40] Alicia: That matches our earlier note; we'll aim for 2026-06-09 22:00 UTC.
[04:44] Marcus: Good. On security, our infosec asked for SOC2 summary and KMS flow. Diego, can you point to the KMS doc?
[04:52] Diego: Yes — we have a short KMS integration guide for both customer-managed keys and Redwood-managed keys. We'll attach that and the SOC2 summary to the shared folder. Note: audit logs can be exported to your SIEM — Marcus, is that what you need?
[05:03] Marcus: Yes, but also field-level retention — we need to understand token retention and whether ephemeral logs can be purged within our retention window.
[05:09] Alicia: We'll include the log retention knobs and an example purge policy in the doc.
[05:13] Priya: Great. A couple of data questions: Do you persist prompt context server-side?
[05:18] Diego: We keep ephemeral KV cache entries for inference speed but we don't persist transcripts unless you enable persistent storage. By default, data-at-rest is not stored beyond the session window. We'll include the exact TTL numbers in the doc.
[05:28] Sana: Ok. Back to performance — is there a quick win on our side to reduce tail without paying for Dedicated?
[05:33] Diego: Yes: 1) pre-warm before heavy windows, 2) smooth out client-side burstiness with a small leaky-bucket admission at your edge, 3) increase concurrency per connection rather than creating many short-lived connections. Those reduce KV churn.
[05:46] Priya: We'll try the leaky-bucket and connection pooling first and share traces.
[05:50] Marcus: Regarding metrics, can you provide per-token cost numbers tied to the benchmark runs so we can compare to incumbent unit cost?
[05:57] Alicia: We'll provide that in the cost ladder spreadsheet. Diego will annotate rows for quantized vs fp16 and explain the assumptions (batching levels, tokens per request).
[06:06] Priya: Anything on fallback policy? If Redwood route fails, will it fall back to a cheaper model or to the incumbent?
[06:12] Diego: We have fallbacks to a smaller model variant in the same region, plus a routing policy that can failover to another region. We won't fail over to incumbent automatically (that requires explicit multivendor config).
[06:23] Sana: We might want a temporary failover to incumbent while we ramp. Is that supported?
[06:27] Alicia: It's supported via a custom routing policy we can set up for the pilot. We'll draft that as part of the playbook.
[06:34] Priya: Any known model quality deltas when quantized? We've seen hallucinations spike in other quantized runs.
[06:40] Diego: We ran evals on your prompt set for quality regression: minor token-level deltas in generation, no systematic hallucination increase in the sample. We'll include the eval spreadsheet and tie it to thresholds for rollout. If you want strict quality parity we can hold to less aggressive quantization.
[06:55] Marcus: Good. That helps.
[06:57] Alicia: Quick check: what success criteria are we using to recommend Dedicated versus Hosted?
[07:04] Priya: For us, success is: 1) 20% lower median latency AND 2) p95 below 350 ms under 3x burst, OR 3) unit cost within 10% of incumbent with equal quality. If we meet two of three, we consider Dedicated.
[07:20] Sana: Add: procurement needs a 3-month cost estimate and the list of stakeholders for signoff.
[07:25] Alicia: Noted. We'll include that in the handoff doc.
[07:28] Diego: I'll also capture a routing snippet you can drop into your staging config to run a canary with pre-warm.
[07:34] Priya: Perfect. Anything else on the bench numbers?
[07:36] Diego: One last note — the incumbent had slightly better single-request tail at very low QPS; our advantage grows as concurrency increases because of better kernel utilization and batching. So if your workload is bursty but concurrent, Redwood benefits.
[07:49] Marcus: Good to know.
[07:50] Alicia: Okay final recap, we'll: share routing playbook + quant notes (Alicia/Diego), run head-to-head in eu-central and eu-west (scheduled 2026-06-09 22:00 UTC), send SOC2 + KMS docs, and provide cost ladder. Customer to share burst traces and confirm stakeholders.
[08:07] Priya: Thanks, that lines up. We'll get the traces to you by Friday.
[08:11] Sana: Thanks everyone.
[08:13] Alicia: Thanks all — we'll follow up with calendar invite and docs.
[08:17] [08:17] End of recording

Notes on transcription: occasional mislabels (K V cash vs KV cache), numbers rounded in voice, some cross-talk near 06:30 when routing discussion overlapped.
